Shadow of something that does not yet exist

I noticed this while making a Person/codekiln/GitHub/beans coffee log entry. I had a poem and a scene in mind. I tried to render the scene as an image, but I ran out of time and settled on something that felt close but not right. The image I used was not the thing I had in mind. It was not even a clean approximation. It felt like a shadow of something that had not fully formed. The thing itself did not exist yet in the world or even in my own mind as a stable object.

Shadow of something that does not yet exist

It is not idea then execution then artifact. It is more like a field that gives rise to a direction, and that direction produces a series of attempts. Each attempt changes the field. The direction shifts as I follow it. The artifact is one temporary stabilization in that loop. It is not the goal. It is a trace left behind as the system moves.
Shadow of something that does not yet exist
Shadow of something that does not yet exist

Plato wrote about shadows as copies of real forms. Here the situation is reversed. The form is not fixed or fully known. It is more like what Whitehead would call a process of becoming. He wrote that the many become one and are increased by one. The image is one such increase. It is not a copy of a prior form but a moment in an ongoing process. Deleuze makes a similar distinction between the virtual and the actual. The virtual is real but not yet actual. Each artifact is one actualization among many possible ones.

The system includes me, the tool, and the outputs. Hutchins described cognition as distributed across people and artifacts. The image feeds back into my perception and changes what I am aiming at. Schön described design as a conversation with the materials of a situation. Here the material includes the model itself. The loop is tight. Each projection alters the next vector.

I will call this a shadow of something that does not yet exist. It is a pre-actualization trace. It marks a direction more than a destination. It is useful not because it is correct but because it lets me continue the motion. The work is to stay with the vector and let the field clarify itself over time.

: is a special builtin (POSIX utility name :) that always succeeds and does nothing with the arguments it is given—it is not a comment token. A line like the following still executes; the words after : are operands to that no-op command, not comment text to the parser:
In POSIX shells, is : a comment or a no-op builtin?

People sometimes use that pattern as a pseudo-comment because the command has no side effects when the operands are simple words (avoid redirections, command substitutions, or other expansions you did not intend to run).
In POSIX shells, is : a comment or a no-op builtin?
The same idea applies across common /bin/sh implementations and user shells such as Bash and zsh, and to lean sh clones like dash—all treat : as this no-op builtin.
In POSIX shells, is : a comment or a no-op builtin?
Actual comments in these languages still start with # (to end of line, per shell grammar).
In POSIX shells, is : a comment or a no-op builtin?

Reading other people’s scripts: lines beginning with : are a weak signal you are in a POSIX-style shell script and the author chose a no-op command instead of # (sometimes to keep a line syntactically valid where a # line would not parse the way they want).

The Ploopy Mouse is an open-source device running QMK firmware, renowned for its flexibility and customization. With eight programmable buttons, you can define their functions directly through text-based configuration files, eliminating the need for proprietary software. This mouse is particularly appealing to users who prefer a high degree of control over their hardware.

QMK (Quantum Mechanical Keyboard) Firmware is an open-source project that enables users to customize the functionality of their computer input devices, such as keyboards, mice, and MIDI controllers. It allows for extensive personalization, including remapping keys, creating macros, and defining complex behaviors. QMK supports a wide range of devices and is compatible with various microcontrollers, particularly those in the Atmel AVR and ARM families. The firmware is written in C and is designed to be both powerful and user-friendly, catering to both beginners and advanced users. The project is community-driven, with contributions from developers and enthusiasts worldwide, and is maintained by QMK collaborators and contributors.

Computer Keyboard/VIA is a graphical configuration tool that interfaces with QMK-enabled devices, allowing users to remap keys, program macros, and adjust settings in real-time without recompiling firmware. While VIA was initially developed for keyboards, it has been extended to support other input devices, including certain mice that run QMK firmware. For instance, the Ploopy Mouse is a QMK-powered mouse that is compatible with VIA, enabling users to reprogram its buttons and functions easily.

In summary, QMK serves as the customizable firmware for input devices, providing the foundational capabilities for personalization. VIA acts as a user-friendly interface to modify these settings dynamically, enhancing the accessibility and convenience of configuring QMK-enabled devices.
